title: Analyzing Medical Research Results Based on Synthetic Data and Their Relation to Real Data Results: Systematic Comparison From Five Observational Studies
summary: This paper validates statistical results derived from synthetic electronic medical record data (generated by the MDClone system) against results from real data across five observational clinical studies, finding strong concordance especially with larger sample sizes. It is a methodological validation study in medical informatics, not a synthetic-data-generation method paper itself. The Synthetic Data Vault (Patki et al. 2016) is cited only in the introduction and discussion as prior background literature on synthetic health data validation, with no SDV code or component run.

title: A Comparative Study of Machine Learning and Spatial Interpolation Methods for Predicting House Prices
summary: This study compares neural networks, random forests, inverse distance weighting, and kriging for predicting missing house price values using real estate transaction data from Seoul, South Korea. The empirical analysis finds that machine learning methods (neural networks, random forests) outperform traditional spatial interpolation techniques, with random forests performing slightly better. CTGAN is cited only in the reference list, with no evidence it was run or engaged with in the text.
evidence: CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) appears only as reference 43 in the bibliography; the full text contains no SDV-family term outside the reference list.

title: Gene–environment pathways to cognitive intelligence and psychotic-like experiences in children
summary: This eLife study uses large-scale longitudinal data from the Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development Study (6,602 children) and a novel structural equation modeling method to test how genetic polygenic scores and familial/neighborhood environmental factors jointly shape cognitive intelligence and childhood psychotic-like experiences, adjusting for confounders. The authors note elsewhere that a synthetic dataset was generated with conditional GAN to imitate the structure of their final study sample, but a full-text search found no further engagement with the method beyond this citation. CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) is cited only in passing as the source of the conditional GAN technique used to produce that synthetic dataset, with no described running or evaluation of the library itself in the retrievable text.

title: When Are Two Scores Better Than One? Investigating Ensembles of Diffusion Models
summary: This paper investigates whether ensembling unconditional score-based diffusion models improves generative modelling, finding gains in score-matching loss and likelihood but inconsistent improvement in perceptual quality metrics like FID, and extends the analysis to tabular data via Random Forest diffusion ensembles. It also provides theoretical results on summing score models relevant to ensembling and guidance. CTGAN (Xu et al., 2019) is cited only as the source of the 'efficiency' metric used to evaluate Random Forest results on tabular data, without running the CTGAN model itself.
evidence: "we evaluate Random Forest using the Wasserstein distance between the generated and test data, coverage (Naeem et al., 2020), and efficiency (Xu et al., 2019), with results reported in Tables 8, 12 and 13."
